content:
Yes. For a class type like std::string, the declaration

std::string myString;

performs default-initialization, which calls std::string's default constructor and yields an empty string.

(For completeness: built-in types behave differently — default-initialized locals are indeterminate, whereas value-initialization like std::string myString{} or std::string myString = std::string(); also produces an empty string.)
